To debug why an IPSec VPN tunnel is only functioning in one direction between a security appliance and another vendor's device, follow these broad steps:

1. **Check Configuration**: Verify the configuration settings on both ends of the tunnel. Ensure that the encryption and hashing algorithms, as well as the pre-shared keys, match on both devices.

2. **Examine Logs**: Review the logs on both the security appliance and the other vendor's device. Look for any error messages or indications of failed negotiations.

3. **Firewall Rules**: Ensure that the firewall rules on both devices allow traffic in both directions. Check for any rules that might be blocking incoming or outgoing traffic.

4. **NAT Issues**: If either device is behind a NAT, ensure that NAT traversal is enabled and properly configured. This can often cause issues with VPN tunnels.

5. **Routing**: Verify that the routing is correctly set up on both ends. Ensure that the traffic is being routed to the correct IP addresses and that there are no routing loops or misconfigurations.

6. **MTU Settings**: Check the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) settings on both devices. Mismatched MTU settings can lead to packet fragmentation issues, which may affect the tunnel.

7. **Rekeying and Timeouts**: Look into the rekeying settings and timeout values. If one side is set to a much shorter timeout, it may cause the tunnel to drop unexpectedly.

For the extra credit regarding two security appliance clusters connected to the same network:

1. **Cluster Configuration**: Ensure that both clusters are configured with unique cluster IP addresses and that they are properly set up to handle failover and load balancing.

2. **Routing and Subnetting**: Make sure that the routing is correctly configured so that traffic can reach both clusters without conflicts. Use different subnets if necessary to avoid overlap.

3. **VPN Configuration**: If the clusters need to establish VPN tunnels, ensure that the VPN configurations are set up correctly on both clusters, including any necessary adjustments for cluster-aware settings.

4. **Health Checks**: Implement health checks to monitor the status of both clusters and ensure that they can communicate effectively with each other and with external networks.

You could use a reverse proxy. In that case, you would assign the NAT address to the reverse proxy device and set up a rule that basically says something like:

* If HTTP HOST header is host1.example.com then forward all requests to 192.168.1.50
* If HTTP HOST header is host2.example.com then forward all requests to 192.168.1.51

This could be some sort of Application Delivery Controller (like a well-known brand), or an open-source solution like NGINX or Apache with mod_proxy.

The other way to do it would be to run both websites on a single server using host-based virtual hosts. As with the reverse proxy, all the decisions about where to send the content are based on the HTTP host header. 

If you are using HTTPS, it becomes slightly more complicated as you need to use either SNI (which limits support for legacy clients) or a wildcard certificate (which only works if both sites use the same root domain; for example, site1.example.com and site2.example.com would both work with a single *.example.com wildcard, but site1.example1.com and site1.example2.com would not work as there is no commonality between them that you could have a wildcard certificate for) as the browser needs to do the SSL handshake before you can read the HTTP request header.

FTP is another protocol that is somewhat similar to this.

Unless you want to open a large range of ports (i.e. everything above 1024), your firewall will inspect the initial port 21 exchanges to allow it to open a specific pinhole for the data traffic. This is why FTPS won't work through firewalls correctly without some significant adjustments being made, as the firewall cannot inspect the initial data connection due to it not being in cleartext and therefore cannot open the pinholes to allow the data traffic through.

So before you add that access list, your internal interface has a security setting of 100, your demilitarized zone (DMZ) 10, and your external 0, so the internal can communicate with everything.

As soon as you apply that access-list to the internal interface, the firewall *only* obeys the access-list, and there is an explicit drop at the end, so anything that isn't specifically allowed is denied.

    access-list DMZ_nat extended permit ip [internal IP] 255.255.255.255 [external IP] 255.255.255.255

If the network switch port is configured as a trunk carrying a specific VLAN, then you will need to configure the VLAN interface with a tag (which is essentially the equivalent of setting up your interface as a single VLAN trunk).

If the switch port is an access port in that VLAN, then you do not need to configure a VLAN interface on your firewall, just a normal interface with no VLAN information.

Trunking is just a way of saying that you can have multiple VLANs on a single interface; in the non-switch world, this is (usually) achieved by having multiple VLAN sub-interfaces with the requisite VLAN.

As this is a firewall, you will generally need an "inside" and an "outside" VLAN/interface/zone. It sounds like the administrator will assign the "other" ports in the facility into the "inside" VLAN, and then the outside of your firewall would connect into the "outside" VLAN.

You would need to enable DHCP on the inside VLAN interface for your PCs, then the firewall will route via the outside interface to the rest of the network. It's possible that the outside interface could be a DHCP client interface, or the administrator will give you a static IP to assign to that.

As it sounds like you only have a single port for your firewall, you will have to essentially configure it as a physical "on a stick." You would have the two VLANs (outside and inside) configured on the same physical interface. Traffic will come from your client PCs to their local switch port on the "inside" VLAN, across the switch infrastructure to the inside VLAN interface of your firewall, the firewall then processes the traffic according to its firewall rules, then sends it outbound via the "outside" VLAN.
